title: Well-conditioned iterative methods for large open quantum systems
authors: Gaspard Beugnot, Paul Gregory, Rémi Robin, Antoine Tilloy
abstract: Markovian open quantum systems are well modeled by the Lindblad Master Equation (ME) $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} ρ_t = \mathcal{L} ρ_t$, where $\mathcal{L}$ is a linear (super-)operator and $ρ_t$ is the system state, a positive matrix. When designing or characterizing a quantum system, one is usually interested in the steady state $ρ_\infty$ (such that $\mathcal{L} ρ_\infty = 0$), the first few excited states, and trajectories $t\mapsto ρ_t$. In finite dimension, $ρ_t$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, $\mathcal{L}$ thus typically costs $n^4$ to store explicitly as a dense matrix, and $O(n^6)$ to diagonalize or invert exactly, making standard linear algebraic techniques expensive for large systems. However, $\mathcal{L}$ usually costs only $O(n^3)$ to apply. This makes iterative methods appealing, but they do not work without a good preconditioner. In this article, our main observation is that a part of the Lindblad equation, corresponding to the so-called no-jump evolution $\mathcal{S}$, can be inverted efficiently. Using this inverse map, we introduce an auxiliary completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) map $Φ$ whose fixed point is directly related to $ρ_\infty$, all the other eigenvalues having smaller magnitude. The map $Φ$ is thus well suited to iterative methods, and $ρ_\infty$ can be found in a few Arnoldi iterations. Using the same inverse map $\mathcal{S}^{-1}$ as preconditioner, we compute the low-lying spectrum efficiently via shift-invert Arnoldi, and, as a proof of concept, build an implicit time integrator that is competitive on stiff systems in the low-precision regime. For the steady-state and low excited states problems, our methods scale like $O(n^3)$ per iteration and offer state-of-the-art performance on CPU and GPU.
summary: This paper tackles the computational challenge of simulating large open quantum systems governed by the Lindblad Master Equation. It introduces a novel numerical approach by decomposing the Liouvillian operator and constructing an auxiliary map $\Phi$ whose fixed point yields the steady state. By leveraging the efficient invertibility of the no-jump evolution part, the authors achieve state-of-the-art, scalable iterative solvers for finding steady states and low-lying spectra.
main_problem: Developing efficient, well-conditioned iterative methods to solve for the steady state, low-lying spectrum, and time evolution of large open quantum systems.
main_result: The authors propose using an auxiliary CPTP map $\Phi$ derived from the no-jump evolution part of the Lindbladian, allowing the steady state to be found efficiently via Arnoldi iterations.
method: The core method involves decomposing the Lindblad operator $\mathcal{L} = S + K$ and utilizing the efficient inversion of the no-jump part $S$ to construct a suitable iterative map $\Phi$. This map is then used with Krylov subspace methods (Arnoldi/GMRES) for convergence.
model_or_system: The system is modeled by Markovian open quantum systems governed by the Lindblad Master Equation ($\dot{ho}_t = \mathcal{L} ho_t$). The analysis focuses on the superoperator $\mathcal{L}$ acting on the density matrix $ho_t$.
key_observables: Steady state $ho_\infty$, low-lying excited states (eigenvectors/eigenvalues of $\mathcal{L}$), and time evolution $ho(t)$.
important_parameters: System dimension $n$ (large, $n \ge 10^3$), time step $\Delta t$, and the spectral gap of $\mathcal{L}$.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the no-jump part $S$ is invertible, which allows the construction of the auxiliary map $\Phi$. The methods are benchmarked assuming a unique steady state exists.
figures_summary: Figures compare spectra of $\mathcal{L}$ and the auxiliary map $\Phi$, showing the latter has eigenvalues confined within the unit circle, which is ideal for iterative solvers.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the computational bottleneck of the Lindblad equation ($\mathcal{L}$), then introduces the decomposition $\mathcal{L} = S + K$. It then details the use of the inverse map $S^{-1}$ to define $\Phi$, showing how $ho_\infty$ relates to the fixed point of $\Phi$, and finally applies this framework to compute the spectrum and time evolution using specialized Krylov solvers.
why_interesting: This work provides state-of-the-art numerical techniques for simulating complex open quantum dynamics, moving beyond the prohibitive $O(n^6)$ scaling of direct methods to an efficient $O(n^3)$ scaling per iteration.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Spectra of a random dense Lindbladian (see section 2.3.1) for a Hilbert space of dimension n = 6. (a) Spectrum of L; even for low-dimensional systems, the large spread of eigenvalues reflects the poor conditioning of L. (b) Spectrum of Φ = −KS−1; all eigenvalues lie within the unit circle (dashed). In both panels, the red star marks the eigenvalue corresponding to the steady state.

Figure 2: Runtime of steady-state solvers versus Hilbert-space dimension n, for the dense random Lindbladian (left) and the memory–buffer cat qubit (right). Our two methods (Arnoldi on Φ and preconditioned GMRES) beat all competitors on CPU, and further gain a ×50 speedup on the H100 GPU; the competitors (QuTiP SVD and ILU-GMRES, MUMPS, Krylov.jl GMRES) run on the Xeon CPU, and the time-evolution baseline on GPU for the cat family. See section B in the Appendix for the exact configurations.

Figure 3: Runtime of resolvent solvers for (λ −L)(ρ) = Id/n versus Hilbert-space dimension n, at the three shifts λ = λmax, λmax/10, λmax/100 (columns), for the dense random Lindbladian (top) and the memory–buffer cat qubit (bottom). Our preconditioned GMRES is shown on CPU (dashed) and on the H100 GPU (solid); the competitors (dense LU, MUMPS, GMRES, GMRES + ILU) run on the Xeon CPU. The gain over the competitors is small at λ = λmax and grows as λ →0, and is largest for the dense family and on GPU. See section B for the exact configurations.

Figure 4: Random dense Lindbladian (section B.1) spectra for a Hilbert space of size n = 6. (a) Full spectrum of L. (b) Spectrum of eLη = L + η Tr (·) Id with η = 10/n, which shifts the steady-state eigenvalue to ηn = 10 (orange star) while leaving all nonzero modes unchanged. (c) Spectrum of eL−1 η : the low-lying modes of eLη (small |λ|) become its dominant eigenvalues (large |1/λ|). The operator actually iterated in the text is (µ −eLη)−1, which at µ = 0 differs from eL−1 η by an overall sign. In all panels, the red star marks the steady state, the green star the slowest-decaying nonzero mode, and the purple stars the next conjugate pair. The orange star in the second and third panels...

Figure 5: Wall-clock time to compute the low-lying spectrum as a function of the Hilbert-space dimension n (log–log), for the dense random Lindbladian (left, section B.1) and the memory– buffer cat qubit (right, section B.1). Our shift-invert Arnoldi solver (SI Arnoldi, ours) is compared against the dense eigenvalues solver of NumPy and the ARPACK shift-invert solver of SciPy, both applied to the n2 × n2 Liouvillian. See section B for the exact configurations.
